newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-Portugal's central bank cuts interest rates.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Portugal's central bank cuts interest rates.

text.p: The Bank of Portugal cut 0.20 percent off interest rates on Monday signalling its confidence that Portugal will make Europe's monetary union, analysts said.

Once again, the Bank wrong-footed market analysts by reducing its repurchase pact rate to 5.5 percent, from 5.7 percent previously, and by lowering its absorption rate -- the level at which it drains funds -- to 5.2 percent.
Interest rate cuts had been predicted, but only for later in the year, with seven out of eight analysts polled earlier on Monday by Reuters excluding an immediate fall.

Most had expected that the central bank would wait until at least next month, particularly as foreign exchange markets have been more volatile of late and there are fears that Germany could even raise rates because of concerns over inflation.
"Despite there being room for the cut, in terms of timing, it was a surprise," said Nuno Godinho of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Lisbon.
"The Bank, like most people, seems pretty optimistic about convergence (to the single currency,)" he added.

Banco Portugues de Investimento chief economist Rui Martins dos Santos also saw the cut as part of a strategy to bring local rates closer to those of Germany because the Bank discounted the country's membership of economic and monetary union (EMU).

Portugal is on target to meet most of the entry requirements for the single currency and investors have become increasingly convinced that it will form part of the first wave of countries to launch EMU on January 1, 1999.

"It corresponds to the objective of the Bank of Portugal of a slow convergence with rates that will exist within the euro (single currency)," said Rui Martins dos Santos, chief economist at Banco Portugues de Investimento.
Despite the cut, Portuguese interest rates still remain slightly above those of neighbouring Spain, whose central bank has a repurchase pact rate of 5.25 percent.
Spain is also regarded as a strong candidate for the single currency where the difference between interest rates charged in member countries will all but disappear.
The gap between Portugal and Germany has fallen to around 0.70 percent for the more internationally traded 10-year bonds but it remains at some 1.5 percent for two-year bonds.
The central bank's decision to cut interest rates followed news last week that Portugal's inflation had slowed again to a year-on-year rate of 1.7 percent in July, down from 1.8 percent in June.

Analysts said that the Bank was not only demonstrating its confidence about monetary union but also sending a message to markets that they should not become alarmed even if Germany felt forced to raise its rates.
The Bundesbank warned recently of signs of some rekindling of inflation, adding that containing inflation remained its top policy priority.
"Regardless of what happens with the German repo, there continues to be room in Portugal for rate cuts and that is the Bank's principal message," said Godinho.
